interactions.summary: Jiang turns the angel scene into a class question: students first identify the angels as protecting the valley from the serpent, then Jiang pushes further until the class recognizes that the imagery means Purgatory is already tied to Eden and still exposed to temptation.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang-led question sequence with multiple student answers

claims.claim: Jiang reads the two angels with flaming swords as a deliberate Genesis echo that forces the class to ask why Edenic guardians appear inside the purgatorial landscape.
A student answer Jiang accepts is that self-reflection and beauty in Purgatory do not remove temptation; the snake remains a live presence and evil can still threaten the scene.
Jiang insists that the snake is not a past symbol only: 'the snake is eternal,' so even purified ascent still unfolds under recurrent threat.
The class arrives at Jiang's next step when a student states that they are effectively in Eden already, which explains why angelic guards and serpent imagery belong in this region of Mount Purgatory.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang refuses the comforting version of Purgatory in one blunt line: the snake is eternal.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the snake will always be there, okay? the snake is eternal
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves the lecture's pressure that temptation is not left behind simply because the soul has turned upward.

signature_moments.moment: A student snaps the symbolism into place by realizing the class is already standing in Edenic space.
signature_moments.source_phrase: we're in the Garden of Eden right now
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The packet pivots on that recognition: Purgatory is not merely a path back to innocence but a geography that already touches it.

chronology_notes.note: The lecture moves from descriptive reading to symbolic interpretation: anti-Purgatory's guarded valley is re-read as Eden-adjacent territory where temptation remains active rather than a fully safe zone.
